lb.note: The layer 7 flavour is the external Application Load Balancer. Google groups every load balancer under one product name and distinguishes them by type rather than selling them separately.

service.note: A plain virtual machine, chosen here because the sizes are the thing a student is picking. Cloud Run is the same workload without the machine choice, and GKE is the same workload with a cluster around it.

db.note: The managed relational database a student reaches for first. Spanner is the other choice and is a different lesson: it scales horizontally and costs accordingly, so it is not the default here.

cache.note: Memorystore also comes in Valkey, Memcached and Redis Cluster flavours. Plain Redis is the one a student means by "add a cache".

queue.note: Cloud Tasks rather than Pub/Sub, because a queue in this sense has a named worker at the other end. Google draws the same line: with Cloud Tasks "a publisher specifies an endpoint where each message is to be delivered", while a Pub/Sub publisher needs to know nothing about its subscribers.

worker.note: A job runs its work and exits, which is what a background worker does. Google contrasts it with a Cloud Run service, which "listens for and serves requests". Cloud Run worker pools fit a queue consumer even better, but they are still in preview, so the stable answer is the one named here.

coldstorage.note: Not a separate product. Archive is one of Cloud Storage's storage classes, alongside Rapid, Standard, Nearline and Coldline, and it carries a 365 day minimum storage duration.

searchindex.note: Google has no managed Elasticsearch or OpenSearch of its own, which is the honest answer for a student who wants a search index you operate. Agent Search is the first-party product for searching your own data, and it is a retrieval service rather than an inverted index. Its own docs list six former names, including Vertex AI Search and Enterprise Search, so expect older material to call it something else.

timeseriesdb.note: No dedicated time series database exists at Google. Bigtable is the usual home for the workload, and Google lists "time-series data, such as CPU and memory usage over time for multiple servers" among its uses, but it is a wide-column store rather than a time series product.

graphdb.note: A feature of Spanner rather than a standalone graph database, and it needs the Enterprise or Enterprise Plus edition. Google has nothing that corresponds to a dedicated graph service.

vectordb.note: The dedicated vector index, renamed from Matching Engine and still carrying that name in some client library classes. If the vectors live beside relational data, pgvector on Cloud SQL or AlloyDB is the other route and avoids running a second system.

streambroker.note: Real Kafka, run by Google, for when the lesson is specifically Kafka. Pub/Sub covers the same shape of problem without the Kafka API.

pubsub.note: Written without a "Cloud" prefix. Publishers "trigger subscriber execution just by publishing an event", which is the distinction from Cloud Tasks.

websocket.note: Google sells no dedicated WebSocket product the way a gateway with a WebSocket mode would be. Cloud Run supports them "with no additional configuration required", holding a stream open for as long as the request timeout, up to 60 minutes.

apigateway.note: The small, cheap one for putting an API in front of serverless backends. Apigee is the other product and is a full API management platform, which is a different scale of decision.

lambda.note: Renamed from Cloud Functions. Google folded the functions product into Cloud Run, so the name a student sees today is this one.

ratelimiter.note: Rate limiting is a policy on the load balancer edge rather than a component you place. Cloud Armor offers throttling to a configured threshold and rate-based bans.

replica.note: Google recommends keeping direct read replicas to ten or fewer, and that is guidance rather than an enforced limit, so no number is stored here.

shard.note: The closest thing to sharding you do not operate yourself. Spanner splits data automatically rather than asking you to choose a shard key the way a sharded Cloud SQL fleet would.

edgecompute.note: Not a general edge runtime, so this is a partial match rather than an equivalent. Service Extensions run your own WebAssembly inside the load balancer, which suits rewriting a header and not hosting an application. The load balancer extensions are generally available; the Media CDN ones are still in preview.
